Folder structure Overview

Your submission should be organised around a valid R package structure first, then place your report and supporting files into the appropriate package locations so they do not interfere with package build/check.

Core principle

Build a standard R package (for Exercise 5), and treat your report materials (qmd, bibliography, any vignette assets) as vignette/article content inside the package, not as loose files scattered around the project. This keeps the package installable and ensures check() behaves as expected.

What goes where

1. Package root (top level)

Your R package must live at the top level of your project (the folder you open in RStudio). This top-level folder should be a standard, installable R package, with all files placed in appropriate package locations.

Include a working .Rproj file at the package root so the marker can open the project and immediately be in the correct working directory. The intent is that the .Rproj sets the base directory and your code can use here::here() to reliably find files.

In your final submission zip, include the entire package folder (not just selected files), so the package can be installed and checked as-is.

2. Vignette/article files

If you are attempting Exercise 5, place your single qmd source file inside: vignettes/article/.

Create this structure correctly using: usethis::use_article() in Console.

This is important because it generates the correct structure; manually creating folders with the same name may not behave the same way.

Also place in the same folder:

  • your .bib references file (for the report)
  • any report assets you need (for example images), if relevant

3. Data files

Put data in one of these locations, depending on its role:

  • Package dataset(s) you want to include as part of the package: follow standard package conventions (for Exercise 5 you are explicitly adding the provided dataset and documenting it).

  • Raw/source data for processing: data-raw/ is acceptable.

  • Data needed only for the report/vignette rendering: may be placed in vignettes/article/.

Notes about check()

When you run check() for your package, you may see a message about deleting an empty vignettes folder even if you have files under vignettes/article/. That message is expected, and you do not need to fix anything.

What to include in the final zip

Submit a single zip named firstname_lastname_SID_Assignment2.zip containing:

  • your Exercise 5 package, including the .Rproj

  • vignettes/article/ containing:

    • one .qmd file
    • one .bib file
    • any supporting files you used for the report (as needed)

  • any data files placed under data-raw/ and/or vignettes/article/ as appropriate

This structure keeps the package compliant and reduces the chance that report files disrupt installation or package checks.

Exercise 1 [10 marks]

As the output of this exercise, you are required to submit your code and its output under a section in your qmd file.

The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is an international assessment measuring student performance in reading, mathematical and scientific literacy.

PISA assesses the extent to which 15-year-old students have acquired some of the knowledge and skills that are essential for full participation in society, and how well they are prepared for lifelong learning in the areas of reading, mathematical and scientific literacy.

In 2022, PISA involved 80 countries and 610,000+ students worldwide. The records for a subset of countries are saved in the pisa_2022.csv file and contain the following variables:

variable class description
country character 3-letter country code.
gender character Gender of the student. Only ‘male’ and ‘female’ are recorded.
math double Simulated score in mathematics.
read double Simulated score in reading.
science double Simulated score in science.

Exercise 2 [10 marks]

As the output of this exercise, you are required to submit your code and its output under a section in your qmd file.

The inspiration for this exercise comes from https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MSPUS. The two datasets you’ll use are aus_median_house_price.csv and aus_GDP_changes.csv, both of which are available on iLearn.

Please note that aus_median_house_price.csv is considered as a wild-caught dataset as it was downloaded directly from this ABS website without any further cleaning/wrangling by us: https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/economy/price-indexes-and-inflation/total-value-dwellings/latest-release.

Please also note that the GDP changes data in aus_GDP_changes.csv is recorded as percentages.

For this question, you need to:

  1. Load the two datasets using read_csv().
  2. [1 mark] Tidy/clean up aus_median_house_price.csv in R. We are only interested in the Melbourne Median Price of Established House Transfers (Unstratified) data in the file.
  3. [4 marks] Create the following visualisation.

  1. [1 mark] Identify periods of very low to negative GDP growth (defined as GDP change of less than 0.1 (%)) that occurred during the time frame of the aus_median_house_price dataset. Do this by adding a new variable that takes the value TRUE if a low GDP growth period occurred during this time frame and FALSE if not. Only keep the records after 1 March 2002, which is the first date for which Melbourne median house price series is available in aus_median_house_price.

  2. [4 marks] Now recreate the following visualisation. The shaded areas should represent periods with very low GDP growth that occurred during the time frame of the aus_median_house_price dataset.

TipHint

There are many ways to create these shaded areas, and you will get full marks as long as you can match the general look and layout of the plot. geom_rect() was used in the plot.

Exercise 3 [10 marks]

As the output of this exercise, you are required to submit your code and its output under a new section in your qmd file.

Recall the Movie database we created in Week 7 SGTA. The code and relevant csv files for this exercise can be found there.

  1. [5 marks] Write dbplyr code and show its output to identify the most common director–actor partnerships in the database.
  2. [5 marks] Consider the following SQL query:
SELECT
  "Name.x",
  COUNT(DISTINCT "Name.y") AS unique_directors,
  COUNT(*) AS total_movies
FROM (
  SELECT
    actors.ActorID AS ActorID,
    actors."Name" AS "Name.x",
    CastingID,
    castings.MovieID AS MovieID,
    "Character",
    Title,
    "Year",
    movies.DirectorID AS DirectorID,
    directors."Name" AS "Name.y"
  FROM actors
  LEFT JOIN castings
    ON (actors.ActorID = castings.ActorID)
  LEFT JOIN movies
    ON (castings.MovieID = movies.MovieID)
  LEFT JOIN directors
    ON (movies.DirectorID = directors.DirectorID)
) q01
GROUP BY "Name.x"
ORDER BY unique_directors DESC

Translate this query into dbplyr syntax and execute it to obtain the output. Briefly discuss what insights can be drawn from the results. Alternatively, you may frame your response by considering what kind of question could have motivated such a query.

Exercise 4 [40 marks]

As the output of this exercise, you are required to submit your report under a new section or multiple sections in your qmd file.

In this question, we are going to compare two methods used in the analysis of 2-by-2 contingency tables. One is the chi-squared test, and the other is the Fisher's exact test.

We will use this example based on the one from the Fisher's exact test Wiki page. A sample of teenagers might be divided into male and female on the one hand and those that are and are not currently studying for a statistics exam on the other. For simplicity, we will be conducting a two-sided test, i.e. testing whether the proportion of studying individuals is the same for both genders or not. The observed frequencies are

Men Women
Studying 3 27
Not-studying 33 9

As output, you need to include your report/write up as part of your qmd file with the appropriate sections/dividers.

You can solve this exercise at different levels. Please state in your report which level you are aiming for.

  • Pass [0-20 marks]: Produce an qmd file that will generate a reproducible html report describing/summarising the chi-squared test and its application. You can use the example above as an illustration. You are welcome to base this on the notes you had from your 1000 level Statistics units and the Wikipedia page about the \(\chi^2\) test, but please do not copy the content from the Wikipedia page directly. Make sure you use the function that matches the method described in your report. You should also include multiple citations, including at least one journal article, one book and one package (if you used a package, you can cite it even they are not \(\chi^2\) test related).
    To achieve full marks for a Pass level attempt, we expect

    • your report to be a part of an qmd file that formatted correctly with no compiling errors
    • all R code will be run in the background and not be visible on your final report;
    • correct usage of the section/ordered list/unordered list environment;
    • all mathematical expressions & tables will be typeset appropriately in your qmd file;
    • at least 3 correctly formatted citations, including one book, one journal & one package;
    • an appropriate summary of the statistical concepts underpinning a \(\chi^2\) test.

  • Credit [21-26 marks]: As at the pass level, but more tasks are handled by R

    • All calculations/results will be handled/populated by R;
    • All citations & in-line references are generated from a BibTex file.

  • Distinction [27-32 marks]: As at the credit level, but added another (sub-)section based on the Fisher's exact test.

    • Once again, you have to describe/summarise the method and use the provided dataset to illustrate. You can base this on its Wikipedia page https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%27s_exact_test but please do not copy the content from the Wikipedia page directly.

  • High Distinction [33-40 marks]: As at the distinction level, but added another (sub-)section and investigate this statement from the Fisher’s exact test’s Wikipedia page: “Despite the fact that Fisher’s test gives exact p-values, some authors have argued that it is conservative, i.e. that its actual rejection rate is below the nominal significance level.”

    Your task is to investigate the above statement by conducting a simulation study. You have to generate 10,000 2-by-2 contingency tables in 4 different settings (so 40,000 in total). Using the terminology as the example we had above, and the 4 different settings are:

    • Setting 1 (Small sample size, small \(p\)): There will be a fixed 20 Men and 20 Women at each iteration and then a 20% success rate of those to be randomly allocated to the Studying group.
    • Setting 2 (Small sample size, normal \(p\)): There will be a fixed 20 Men and 20 Women at each iteration and then a 50% success rate of those to be randomly allocated to the Studying group.
    • Setting 3 (Large sample size, small \(p\)): There will be a fixed 100 Men and 100 Women at each iteration and then a 20% success rate of those to be randomly allocated to the Studying group.
    • Setting 4 (Large sample size, normal \(p\)): There will be a fixed 100 Men and 100 Women at each iteration and then a 50% success rate of those to be randomly allocated to the Studying group.

    For each contingency table, run both the \(\chi^2\) test and Fisher’s exact test and collect their \(P\)-values. You can then compare the rejection proportion based on three significance levels: 10%, 5% and 1%. Summarise your findings.

WarningSome important notes/requirements for Question 4
  • In Setting 1, you may end up with no student in the “Studying” group by chance. Your code will have to check and replace such a sample if it happens.
  • In Settings 1 & 2, you can ignore any warning messages when the assumption for the \(\chi^2\) test is not satisfied.

Exercise 5 [20 marks]

Your task for this exercise is to create an R package using the script Multiserver.R (available on iLearn), which is used to simulate how customers will go through a first come, first serve queuing system as long as “fate” has already decided when each customer will arrive and their service times.

For those who are interested in the logic behind Multiserver.R, we can use bankmodel.xlsx (available on iLearn) to illustrate a queuing system in a bank. Notice that those times can be regenerated, so the numbers on the spreadsheet may differ from those shown below.

We want to calculate the times at which each customer’s service time starts and ends. Consider Customer 6. The highlighted times show when the three servers will become available after dealing with Customers 1 through 5.

Server 2 becomes available at time 450.56, earlier than the other two servers, so we determine that Customer 6 will go to Server 2 (and that is shown in cell I8).

However, Customer 6’s service does not start at time 450.56–because, at that time, Customer 6 hasn’t arrived yet! Cell J8 is later of cells B8 and F8, i.e., the transaction begins when the customer and server are both ready.

Adding the transaction duration (from cell C8) gives the time shown in K8, when the transaction finishes and Customer 6 leaves the bank. Lastly, that time, 648.25, becomes the new next-available time for Server 2 and is copied down to cell F9.

The tabular simulation fully describes the comings and goings of customers through the system. We could then use this simulation to answer various questions about the system. For instance, how would we calculate the average time that each customer had to wait in the queue? Also, adding another server to the system would reduce the average waiting time, but by how much? Feel free to explore the answers to these questions, but they are not part of this assignment.

All we need at this stage is some arrival and service times. To get you started, you can find bank.csv on iLearn, which was generated by using the following code.

# to generate 100 customer's arrival time and their service times
set.seed(2048)
# customers arrived according to a Poisson Process
# = inter arrival time has an exponential distribution
# Set arrival rate to one per 60 seconds = mean inter-arrival time is 60s
arrival_time <- cumsum(rexp(100, 1 / 60))
# service time is exponential distributed with mean 150s + 20s greeting
service_time <- rexp(length(arrival_time), 1 / 150) + 20
bank <- data.frame(arrival_time, service_time)

For this question, you have to

  • Create an R package with all the appropriate documentation.
  • Add the bank dataset to your package.
  • Implement testthat with at least 2 expectations or snapshots.
  • Currently we used data.frame() on line 34 in Multiserver(). Change that to tibble() and update the package accordingly.

Classroom 50 Workflow Rubric
Grade Marks Description
Poor 0–4 Single commit and/or push at the end only. Commit messages are missing or uninformative (e.g. “update”, “final”). Little evidence of incremental progress or effective use of Git workflow.
Satisfactory 5–6 Limited commit history (typically 1–2 commits). Messages are present but vague or inconsistent. Some evidence of progress, but changes are mostly bundled rather than committed in logical steps.
Exceeds expectations 7–8 At least 3 meaningful commits with pushes. Commits show incremental development and a basic, consistent Git workflow.
Outstanding 9–10 Multiple well-scoped commits (3+) with regular pushes throughout. Clear, specific messages. Commits reflect logical development stages. Repository is tidy and organised, demonstrating strong version-control habits.
